title: Quickly, not badly
hook: don't say someone bathes badly, say quickly, until you know his reasons (Enchiridion 45)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the reunion, and the step from more to better. Your line was doesn't follow. Which comparison did you catch? Day three hundred eighty.

A man walks into the public baths, washes, and is out the door in ten minutes, while everyone else lingers over the hot water, the oil and the gossip. Everyone notices. And everyone has the same word ready: he bathes badly. Sloppy. Rude. Doesn't know how it's done. Section forty-five of the handbook takes that one word and swaps it for another. It's a tiny edit, and it changes what you're claiming to know. Today: quickly, not badly.
screen: `EVERYONE ELSE LINGERS AT THE BATHS.` → `ONE MAN IS OUT IN TEN MINUTES.` → `QUICKLY, NOT BADLY.`

segments.voice: First, the swap. Someone bathes quickly, Epictetus says. Don't say he bathes badly. Say he bathes quickly. Someone drinks a lot of wine. Don't say he drinks badly. Say he drinks a lot. Second, the reason. Until you know the judgment behind what he's doing, how do you know it's bad? Maybe the quick bather has a sick child at home. Maybe he's late for work, or the water is cold, or he simply doesn't like crowds. You saw the speed. You didn't see the reason. Third, what you gain. If you keep to this, Epictetus says, you won't end up grasping some impressions clearly and then agreeing to others you never actually saw. In plain words: say only what you saw. Quickly is something you saw. Badly is something you added. The habit protects you from a thousand small, confident mistakes about other people. Fourth, a modern echo. A twentieth-century psychologist, Marshall Rosenberg, built a whole approach to hard conversations, which he called Nonviolent Communication, on a similar first step: separate what you observe from how you evaluate it. You came home at midnight is an observation. You're irresponsible is a judgment. Two very different teachers, a long way apart, each with their own reasons, both noticing that people can hear a description without bracing for a fight. A judgment usually starts one. And we met yesterday's cousin of this idea: richer doesn't mean better. Today's version is shorter still. Quickly doesn't mean badly.
screen: `NOT 'BADLY.' 'QUICKLY.'` · `YOU DIDN'T SEE THE REASON.` · `SAY ONLY WHAT YOU SAW.` · `OBSERVE FIRST, EVALUATE LATER.` · then, large: `QUICKLY, NOT BADLY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose habits bother you. The coworker who's always late. The neighbor who mows at seven. The relative who checks their phone at dinner. Notice the word you usually reach for: rude, lazy, thoughtless. Now try Epictetus' swap. Late. Early. Often on the phone. Just the description. Say it inside, and notice what happens to the irritation when the judgment drops out. The bell holds the time.
Quickly. Epictetus' swap: say he bathes quickly, not badly, because you saw the speed, but not the reason. Today's word.
Your line: say what you saw. Once today, describe instead of judging, and leave out what you added. Day three hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism describe other people's actions in plain, observable terms before making any judgment about them, as Epictetus suggests in Enchiridion 45.

myth: Epictetus says to praise everyone's habits
he says describe them. you don't know the reason, so don't call it bad.
Epictetus' second example is someone who drinks a lot of wine
don't say he drinks badly. say he drinks a lot.

fork.setup: your roommate leaves dishes in the sink overnight. what fits Enchiridion 45?
options: the dishes were in the sink overnight.
fork.reveal: describe what you saw. until you know the reason behind it, you don't know it's bad.

original.note: Greek: quickly, the word Epictetus puts in place of 'badly' in Enchiridion 45.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be judgmental.
what it means: describe what you actually saw, quickly, a lot, late, and leave out the verdict you can't see.
what a scholar hears: it's about assent: say 'badly' and you agree to an impression you never clearly grasped.
recall: the ruling part of the mind

sources.ref: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication (observation versus evaluation)

notes: Enchiridion 45 paraphrased: does someone bathe quickly, say not that he bathes badly but quickly; drinks much wine, say not badly but much; before you know the judgment, how do you know it is bad; so you will not comprehend some appearances clearly and assent to others. Confirm.
Roman baths description (rooms, oil, strigil, ball games) is general background; confirm.
